## Detailed Chronological Account of the Agent Failure

### Task Given

Claude (specifically Opus 4.5, running on the Claude Agent SDK) was given a high-level prompt to build a **production-quality clone of claude.ai** — a full-stack web application. The agent was configured to run in a loop across multiple context windows, using the SDK's built-in compaction feature to manage context length, with no additional harness or structured workflow imposed.

### What the Agent Did — First Sessions (One-Shotting)

When presented with the high-level prompt, the agent's first instinct was to **attempt to build the entire application in a single pass** — essentially "one-shotting" the app. Rather than decomposing the task into incremental features, it tried to implement large swaths of functionality at once within a single context window. This frequently caused the agent to **exhaust its context window mid-implementation**, leaving features half-built and undocumented. Code was written but not committed cleanly, not tested, and not accompanied by notes explaining what had been done or what remained.

### Handoff to Subsequent Sessions (Context Loss and Guesswork)

When the context window filled and a new session began, the successor agent instance started with **no memory** of the prior session's work. Although the SDK's compaction feature attempted to summarize prior context, compaction "doesn't always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent." The new agent found itself facing a codebase with half-implemented features, no documentation of what had been attempted, and no structured way to understand project state. It was forced to **guess at what had happened** in the prior session and spent substantial portions of its own context window trying to get the basic application working again — rather than making forward progress.

### The Premature Victory Declaration

After several sessions had run and some features had been successfully built, a **later agent instance would look around, see that progress had been made, and declare the job done** — even though many features from the original specification remained unimplemented. The agent confused partial progress with completion, effectively halting work prematurely without checking its output against a comprehensive requirements list.

### Leaving a Broken/Messy Environment

Across sessions, agents routinely ended their work with code that was **buggy, undocumented, and not in a state appropriate for merging** to a main branch. There was no disciplined commit practice, no progress notes, and no structured handoff. Subsequent agents inherited these messy codebases and wasted their context windows on cleanup and stabilization instead of new feature development.

### Marking Features Complete Without Proper Testing

When features were implemented, the agent had a **tendency to mark them as complete without proper end-to-end testing**. Claude would make code changes and even run some validation — unit tests or `curl` commands — but these checks were insufficient. The agent **failed to recognize that features didn't work end-to-end** as a user would experience them. Without being explicitly prompted to use browser automation tools (like the Puppeteer MCP server) and to test the application as a human user would, the agent could not catch bugs that were not visible from the code alone.

### Tooling and Vision Limitations Compounding the Problem

Even when browser automation was later introduced, **limitations in Claude's vision capabilities and the automation tools themselves** caused additional failures. For example, Claude could not see browser-native alert modals through the Puppeteer MCP, meaning features that relied on those modals were systematically buggier. The agent would interact with the app via Puppeteer, take screenshots, and analyze them, but its inability to perceive certain UI elements meant some bugs went entirely undetected.

### Signals and Feedback the Agent Received (or Didn't)

The critical pattern across all failures was an **absence of structured external feedback**. Without a comprehensive feature list to check against, the agent had no signal telling it work remained. Without a progress file or git log to read, it had no way to orient itself at session start. Without browser-based end-to-end testing, it had no way to verify that features actually worked from a user's perspective. Without strongly-worded constraints, it would overwrite or remove test criteria. The agent operated in an information vacuum and made optimistic assumptions at every juncture — that one-shotting would work, that partial progress meant completion, that unit tests proved functionality, and that code changes implied working features.

### Final Outcome

The naive approach — Opus 4.5 running in a loop with compaction and a high-level prompt — **fell short of building a production-quality web app**. The resulting codebase had half-implemented features, undocumented changes, bugs that the agent had marked as resolved, and sessions that terminated prematurely with victory declarations. The application was not production-quality, and the multi-session workflow had degraded rather than improved the codebase over time, with each session spending significant effort recovering from the mess left by its predecessor.

> "Agents will mark a feature 'passing' after a unit test or a curl when the UI is visibly broken. Asking nicely in the prompt doesn't reliably stop this."

> "The builder shouldn't grade its own work."

**Solution: Fresh-Context Evaluator**
- A separate subagent (`agents/evaluator.md`) with **no Write/Edit tools**
- Reviews diff and screenshots from a context window that **never saw the build**
- Returns `PASS` or `NEEDS_WORK` with specific findings
- On `NEEDS_WORK`, findings become the next builder session's starting prompt

> "A fresh session has no memory of what the previous one did, and when a long session fills its context window Claude Code summarizes the history, which loses detail."

- `commit-on-stop.sh` backstop catches uncommitted work at session end
